plan.title: Woodpecker-Style Nest Box
plan.summary: Build a weather-shedding wooden nest box with a large entrance, a sloped removable roof, and shallow interior climbing kerfs to help nestlings reach the exit. Its dimensions are estimates based on the photo; confirm the entrance size and cavity dimensions suit the bird species in your area before building.
assumptions: The photo is treated as a medium-to-large woodpecker nest box. The estimated cavity is about 200 mm wide, 220 mm deep, and 470 mm high; the 63 mm entrance is only a starting point, not a universal species requirement.
Dimensions are estimated from the photo because no target dimensions or bird species were provided.
Use 18 mm exterior-rated plywood. The gable sides and sloped roof approximate the photo while keeping the cuts practical for a home workshop.

The box is intended to mount to a sturdy wooden post. The post and site-specific mounting hardware are not included in the box dimensions or parts list. For a living tree, use an adjustable tree-safe strap system that allows for trunk growth rather than driving screws into the tree.
Leave the cavity unfinished. Apply exterior finish only to the outside, away from the entrance and interior.
The shallow kerfs inside the front panel are intended as a climbing surface, but local bird-care guidance should be checked for the target species.
clarifying_questions: Which bird species or region should this box be designed for? Entrance diameter and cavity dimensions vary by species.

steps.title: Lay out and cut the panels
steps.text: Mark P1–P8 on the specified stock and cut the panels and blocks to size. Cut P4 and P5 with matching sloped top profiles, and dry-check that the 200 mm-wide front and back fit between the sides. Ask the lumberyard to make straight cuts if needed.
tools_used: Circular saw with straightedge guide or table saw
steps.safety: Wear eye, hearing, and dust protection. Support stock securely and keep hands clear of the blade.
steps.tip: Label inside and outside faces before drilling or cutting the climbing kerfs.

steps.title: Cut the entrance and drainage holes
steps.text: Cut the 63 mm entrance in P2, centered across its width with its center 322 mm above the panel bottom. Drill four small drainage holes near the corners of P1. Smooth the opening without enlarging it.
steps.safety: Clamp the panels before drilling or sawing, and keep hands clear of the hole-saw teeth and blade.
steps.tip: Do not add a perch; it can help predators reach into the nest.

steps.title: Make the climbing surface and prepare joints
steps.text: On the inside face of P2, cut shallow horizontal kerfs about 3 mm deep and 5 mm apart, extending from near the floor to just below the entrance. Keep the kerfs shallow, with no loose mesh, exposed wire, or fastener points protruding into the cavity. Drill pocket holes along the underside perimeter of P1; drill clearance holes in the outside faces of P2 and P3 at each side seam, then make centered pilot holes in the receiving edges of P4 and P5.
tools_used: Drill/driver with countersink and bits for clearance holes and pilot holes
Circular saw with straightedge guide or table saw
steps.safety: Wear eye protection while drilling and dust protection while sanding or cutting. Clamp panels securely before making kerfs.
steps.tip: Keep the front-panel screw holes near the side seams and clear of the entrance; use a depth stop so kerfs do not break through the plywood.

steps.title: Attach the front and back to the floor
steps.text: Spread a thin bead of exterior wood glue along the bottom edges of P2 and P3. Set them on P1 at the front and back edges, clamp them square, and drive three #8 x 32 mm pocket-hole screws through P1 into each panel. Wipe away glue squeeze-out.
steps.safety: Wear eye protection while driving screws and ventilate the work area when using glue.
steps.tip: Check that both panels are perpendicular to the floor before tightening the screws.

steps.title: Install the gable sides
steps.text: Apply exterior wood glue to the bottom and end edges of P4 and P5. Fit the sides outside the ends of P2 and P3, then drive three #8 x 32 mm pocket screws through P1 into each side. From the outside faces of P2 and P3, drive three corrosion-resistant #8 x 38 mm screws per seam through countersunk clearance holes into the centered pilot holes in the side edges. Check the box diagonals for squareness and clamp while the glue cures according to its label.
tools_used: Drill/driver with countersink and bits for clearance holes and pilot holes
steps.safety: Keep the box clamped on a stable bench and wear eye protection while driving screws.
steps.tip: Do not overtighten the exterior screws; stop when the heads are seated in the countersinks and the seams are closed.

steps.title: Fit locating blocks and outdoor roof latches
steps.text: With P6 off the box, glue and fasten P7 and P8 beneath the roof at the positions shown, driving two #8 x 32 mm screws from the roof face into each block. From outside, fasten P7 to P4 and P8 to P5 with two corrosion-resistant #8 x 32 mm screws per block. Install two outdoor draw latches on each side and one each at the front and back, using corrosion-resistant #8 x 16 mm screws; mount each roof leaf to P6 or its backing block and each catch to the outside wall. Test every latch from outside and confirm the roof lifts off completely when all latches are released.
tools_used: Drill/driver with countersink and bits for clearance holes and pilot holes
steps.safety: Wear eye protection and support the roof securely while drilling. Keep fingers clear of latch pinch points.
steps.tip: Do not glue P6 to the box. Confirm the latches can be reached and released from outside before finishing.

steps.title: Mount the box to a suitable support
steps.text: Mount the box to a sturdy wooden post using site-appropriate exterior structural screws through P3 into the post, spaced well apart and driven into sound wood. The post and mounting fasteners are outside the box parts list; select fasteners for the actual post and installation conditions. For a living tree, use an adjustable tree-safe strap system rather than driving screws into the trunk, and allow room for trunk growth.
steps.safety: Use a stable ladder only if needed, have a helper support the box, and do not overreach. Do not climb or stand on the box.
steps.tip: Choose a sheltered location and follow local wildlife guidance for height and orientation.

steps.title: Sand and finish the exterior
steps.text: Lightly sand exterior faces and ease sharp corners. Apply exterior water-based finish to outside faces only, keeping the cavity, climbing kerfs, entrance, and drainage holes clear. Let the finish dry fully according to its label before placing the box in service.
steps.safety: Work with good ventilation, wear gloves as directed by the finish label, and keep finishes away from flames and children.
steps.tip: Inspect the entrance, kerfs, and drainage holes after finishing and clear any coating that blocks them.

safety_overview: Wear safety glasses when cutting, drilling, or driving screws; use hearing protection around power saws.
Wear a dust mask when cutting or sanding plywood, and work with good ventilation.
Clamp and support panels before cutting or drilling; keep hands clear of blades and hole-saw teeth.
Use a stable work surface and get help holding the box during mounting. Do not overreach from a ladder.
Keep exterior finish off the inside cavity and follow the product label for handling and drying.

review.summary: The basic plywood box is practical, but the wall-seam fastening instructions are reversed and the roof blocks permanently connect the supposedly removable roof to the walls. Specify compatible roof latches and revise the assembly details before building.

issues.problem: J13 and J14 glue and screw P7/P8 to the roof, then J15 and J16 glue and screw those same blocks to the walls. This permanently attaches the roof, regardless of whether the latches are released. The instruction to attach the blocks to the walls while the roof is off also conflicts with the preceding assembly.
issues.fix: Keep J13 and J14, but delete J15 and J16 and their four screws from the hardware list. Attach P7/P8 only to P6, leaving their wall-contact faces unglued and unscrewed. Dry-fit the roof with enough clearance for the blocks to slide freely past the walls, then verify complete roof removal before installing the latches.

issues.problem: J5–J8 specify driving through the front and back faces into the side-panel edges, but the stated construction places the sides outside the ends of the front and back panels. Those are not the overlapping faces of these butt joints; the specified screw path does not fasten the seams as intended.
issues.fix: Reverse the fastening direction for J5–J8: drive through clearance holes in the outside faces of P4/P5 into centered pilot holes in the edges of P2/P3. Retain three exterior screws per seam and the exterior glue. Update the drilling instructions in step 3, the driving instructions in step 5, and all four joint descriptions.

issues.problem: J9–J12 specify only generic small draw latches, without establishing how their mounting leaves bridge the sloped roof-to-wall corners. Ordinary coplanar draw latches are not automatically suitable. The instructions also alternate between mounting to the roof and to its backing blocks without defining accessible mounting faces or screw locations.
issues.fix: Select a specific corrosion-resistant latch suitable for the actual roof-to-wall mounting arrangement. Add its mounting template, mounting faces, pilot-hole sizes, and compatible screw specification to step 6. Dry-fit one latch before drilling the remaining locations. If backing is required, provide backing at each affected latch location and attach any roof-side backing only to the removable roof. Update J9–J12 and the hardware list to match the selected product.

issues.problem: Finishing after mounting makes sanding, coating the back, and sealing exposed plywood edges unnecessarily difficult, potentially requiring work from a ladder.
issues.fix: Move exterior sanding and finishing ahead of mounting. With the roof removed, coat accessible exterior faces and exposed exterior plywood edges while keeping the cavity, entrance, drainage holes, and latch mechanisms clear. Allow the finish to dry fully before mounting.

plan.title: Walnut-Look Console Table with Lower Shelf
plan.summary: A long, narrow console table inspired by the photo: a warm, walnut-colored solid-wood top, straight square legs, a simple apron, and a low plywood shelf. The plan uses beginner-friendly pocket-hole joinery and tabletop fasteners that let the solid top move with seasonal humidity changes.
assumptions: The photo does not provide a reliable scale, so this plan estimates a console table at 1500 mm wide × 400 mm deep × 760 mm high.
The table is intended for home display and light serving: plan for up to 45 kg distributed on the top and 25 kg distributed on the shelf; do not sit or stand on it.
Use an edge-glued pine panel for the top, pine for legs and support rails, poplar for the aprons, and 18 mm birch plywood for the shelf. Stain the pine and poplar a walnut color to match the photo.
The top is solid wood with its grain running along the 1500 mm width. Figure-eight tabletop fasteners allow movement across the 400 mm depth.
The lower shelf is flush with the inner faces of the legs at its ends and has 30 mm clearance from the floor.

parts.name: Solid-wood tabletop
parts.buy_spec: 25 mm thick edge-glued pine panel, cut to 1500 × 400 mm
parts.notes: Keep the grain running along the 1500 mm dimension. Sand the faces and edges before applying finish.

parts.name: Legs
parts.notes: Cut four legs from 38 × 38 mm square stock. The 30 mm inset at the front and back gives the top a modest overhang.

parts.name: Front and rear aprons
parts.notes: Rip from 19 × 89 mm stock to 70 mm wide. Each apron sits between the legs and finishes flush with the underside of the top.

parts.name: Left and right aprons
parts.notes: Rip from 19 × 89 mm stock to 70 mm wide. These aprons fit between the front and rear legs.

parts.name: Lower shelf
parts.notes: Square-edged rectangular shelf panel. Its long edges rest on the front and rear support rails.

parts.name: Lower shelf support rails
parts.notes: The rails run between the legs and support the shelf along its front and rear edges.

joints.drive_from: From the inside face of each 19 mm apron, through pocket holes into the side-grain face of the leg.
joints.note: Set the pocket-hole jig for 19 mm stock and use its manufacturer-recommended 32 mm coarse-thread screws. Glue the contact; screws enter leg side grain, not end grain.

joints.drive_from: From the inside face of each 19 mm side apron, through pocket holes into the side-grain face of the leg.
joints.note: Set the pocket-hole jig for 19 mm stock and use its manufacturer-recommended 32 mm coarse-thread screws. Glue the contact; screws enter leg side grain, not end grain.

joints.drive_from: Fit one bracket at each rail end, with one flange against the leg's inner side face and the other under the rail; drive the kit screws into the leg side grain and rail underside.
joints.note: The fixed rail placements overlap each leg by only 19 mm in depth, so do not rely on the partial end contact or pocket screws. The bracket bridges and reinforces this contact; glue the wood contact as well. Use a bracket kit whose included screws are specified for this installation and do not break through the leg or rail. Dry-fit and test one joint on matching offcuts before assembling.

joints.drive_from: From the top face of the shelf, down through the plywood into the centerline of each rail's 38 mm-wide top face.
joints.note: Glue the shelf to the rails. Put four screws along each rail at x positions approximately 250, 550, 950, and 1250 mm; each row must remain centered over the rail's 38 mm width. Pilot-drill and countersink. A 38 mm screw passes through 18 mm plywood and enters the rail about 20 mm, leaving about 18 mm before the rail underside.

fasteners.name: Figure-eight tabletop fastener kit, screws included

joints.drive_from: First mount the apron-side half while the apron edge is exposed; after positioning the base on the inverted top, swing the connector into place and drive only its tabletop-side screw from below.
joints.note: No glue. Install four pivoting connectors on each long apron. Follow the connector maker's recess and pilot-hole instructions. Use only the supplied tabletop screw if its penetration is no more than 15 mm into the 25 mm top; confirm length before driving.

fasteners.name: Figure-eight tabletop fastener kit, screws included

joints.drive_from: First mount the apron-side half while the apron edge is exposed; after positioning the base on the inverted top, swing the connector into place and drive only its tabletop-side screw from below.
joints.note: No glue. Install two pivoting connectors on each side apron. Follow the connector maker's recess and pilot-hole instructions. Use only the supplied tabletop screw if its penetration is no more than 15 mm into the 25 mm top; confirm length before driving.

fasteners.name: Slotted tabletop-clip kit, screws included
fasteners.size: one clip per leg, for a 25 mm solid top

joints.drive_from: Mount each clip's leg-side portion to the upper inside face of a leg while accessible; with the base on the inverted top, swing the slotted portion under the top and drive its supplied short screw from below.
joints.note: No glue. Use clips that permit movement across the tabletop depth. Confirm the supplied top screw penetrates no more than 15 mm into the 25 mm top, and leave the clip free to slide or pivot.

joints.drive_from: At each leg-to-shelf edge contact, apply a small amount of wood glue to the contacting faces while setting the shelf in place.
joints.note: This small edge contact is only to prevent rattling; it is not a shelf support or a load-bearing fastener. The P6 rails carry the shelf. Do not add screws through the shelf edge.

consumables.name: Wood glue
consumables.note: For structural leg-to-apron, leg-to-rail, and shelf-to-rail joints; do not glue the solid tabletop to the aprons.

consumables.name: Sandpaper
consumables.note: Sand progressively; finish with 220 grit before staining.

consumables.name: Walnut-color wood stain
consumables.note: Test on an offcut first; pine can stain unevenly.

consumables.name: Clear water-based polyurethane
consumables.note: Apply two or three thin coats; follow the product label for recoat and cure times.

consumables.name: Wood filler
consumables.note: Optional; use stainable filler only for small visible defects.

steps.title: Check dimensions and cut the stock
steps.text: Confirm the tabletop is 1500 × 400 × 25 mm. Cut P2, P3, P4, and P6 to the fixed part dimensions, then cut P5 to 1348 × 302 mm; label each piece. Dry-fit the frame parts and check that the legs and aprons sit square.
steps.safety: Wear eye and hearing protection when cutting. Support long stock on both sides of the cut and keep hands clear of the blade.
steps.tip: Ask the home center to cut the plywood and top panel if you do not have a suitable saw and guide.

steps.title: Sand the parts while separate
steps.text: Sand exposed faces and edges of the legs, aprons, rails, shelf, and tabletop, working from 120 to 180 and then 220 grit. Ease sharp corners lightly, but keep joint faces square. Remove dust before assembly.
steps.safety: Wear a dust mask and eye protection; use dust collection or work in a well-ventilated area.
steps.tip: Do not round over the tops of the aprons or legs; those faces need to fit tightly against the tabletop.

steps.title: Prepare pocket holes and tabletop connectors
steps.text: Set the pocket-hole jig for 19 mm stock and drill two holes near each end of P3 and P4. Do not drill pocket holes in P6. Route shallow recesses for the figure-eight connectors in the upper apron edges, then install their apron-side halves while the edges are exposed; follow the connector maker's instructions and check that every connector pivots freely. Also mount the leg-side portions of four slotted tabletop clips near the top inside face of P2, one per leg, using the kit instructions; keep the slotted portions accessible for later attachment to the tabletop.
tools_used: Router with a small straight bit
steps.safety: Clamp parts before drilling or routing. Wear eye protection, keep hands clear of bits, and unplug the router before changing bits.
steps.tip: Dry-fit all connectors and clips before assembly. Recesses should be only as deep as their makers specify, with the hardware free to pivot or slide.

steps.title: Assemble the leg-and-apron frame
steps.text: Fit P3 and P4 between the four legs as shown by the fixed placements. Apply wood glue at each leg-to-apron contact, clamp the frame square, and drive two 32 mm coarse-thread pocket-hole screws at each apron end from the apron inside face into the leg face. Check both frame diagonals before the glue sets.
steps.safety: Keep the frame supported on a stable, level surface while clamping and driving screws.
steps.tip: Wipe away squeeze-out promptly and recheck the diagonals; equal diagonal measurements indicate a square frame.

steps.title: Install the lower shelf support rails
steps.text: Position the two P6 rails at their specified locations, y=140 mm, with the ends against the legs. Their fixed placements provide only 19 mm of depth overlap at each leg, so reinforce each rail end with one 50 × 50 mm heavy-duty angle bracket: one flange against the leg's inner side face and one under the rail. Glue the wood contact, install the bracket-kit screws into the leg side grain and rail underside as directed by the manufacturer, and check that both rails are level. Before assembly, dry-fit and test one bracket connection on matching offcuts to confirm screw fit and safe screw lengths.
steps.safety: Support the frame so it cannot tip. Wear eye protection while drilling and verify screw lengths and hole positions before driving.
steps.tip: Do not use a pocket-hole screw for these rail ends; the bracket is the reinforced connection for their partial contact.

steps.title: Fit and fasten the lower shelf
steps.text: Set P5 onto the P6 rails with its ends flush with the inner faces of the legs. Apply a thin bead of wood glue along the rail tops and a small amount at each leg-to-shelf edge contact to prevent rattling; the rails, not those edge contacts, support the shelf. Pilot-drill and countersink four holes along the centerline of each rail, near x=250, 550, 950, and 1250 mm, then drive four 38 mm #8 screws per rail through the shelf into the rail.
steps.safety: Wear eye protection while drilling and keep the panel supported so it cannot slip or tip.
steps.tip: Keep each screw row centered on the 38 mm rail width; a 38 mm screw enters the rail about 20 mm without reaching its underside.

steps.title: Attach the tabletop using movement-friendly hardware
steps.text: Place P1 face down on a clean padded surface and set the base on it with the overhangs aligned. Swing each exposed apron connector into position, pilot-drill to a controlled depth, and install only its tabletop-side screw; use the supplied screw only if its penetration is no more than 15 mm into the top. Connect the four leg clips the same way, using short supplied screws that also penetrate no more than 15 mm; do not glue the solid top to the frame.
steps.safety: Use a helper to turn the assembled table over; support the top evenly and avoid lifting by the aprons alone. Wear eye protection while drilling and use a depth stop or tape mark to control pilot-hole depth.
steps.tip: Confirm every tabletop screw is short enough before driving. The connectors and clips must remain able to pivot or slide as the solid top moves across its depth.

steps.title: Inspect, fill, and do final sanding
steps.text: Set the table upright and check that it stands flat, the shelf is level, and the frame has no wobble. Fill small visible defects if needed, allow filler to dry, then hand-sand filled areas and glue residue with 220-grit paper. Remove all dust before finishing.
steps.safety: Wear a dust mask and eye protection while sanding; keep clear of exposed tabletop hardware.
steps.tip: If the table rocks, mark the long leg and trim only a small amount at a time.

steps.title: Apply the walnut-color stain
steps.text: Test the stain on an offcut, then apply a thin, even coat to the table with a lint-free cloth or brush. Wipe away excess according to the label and let the stain dry fully before clear coating. Keep the table in a dust-free, ventilated place while it dries.
steps.safety: Use stain only with good ventilation, gloves, and eye protection. Keep oily rags away from heat and dispose of them according to the product label.
steps.tip: Pine can absorb stain unevenly; test the full finish schedule on scrap first.

steps.title: Protect the table with clear finish
steps.text: Apply two or three thin coats of water-based polyurethane to the top, legs, aprons, and shelf. Lightly sand between coats with the grit recommended by the finish maker, remove dust, and allow the final coat to cure before placing objects on the table. Follow the label for exact recoat and cure times.
steps.safety: Ventilate the room and wear the finish manufacturer's recommended PPE. Keep wet finish away from flames, children, and pets.
steps.tip: Thin coats are less likely to sag or remain tacky; do not rush the full cure time.

safety_overview: Wear safety glasses during cutting, drilling, routing, and sanding; use hearing protection around power saws and routers.
Use a dust mask or respirator for sanding and finishing, and provide strong ventilation when applying stain or polyurethane.
Clamp stock before cutting, drilling, or routing; keep hands clear of blades and bits and unplug tools before changing bits.
Lift and turn the assembled table with a helper. Do not sit, stand, or climb on the table; keep loads within the stated distributed-load estimates.
Dispose of stain-soaked rags safely according to the product label; some oil-based products can cause rags to heat up and ignite.

review.summary: The plan is buildable for an intermediate woodworker. The apron joinery, supported plywood shelf, and movement-friendly tabletop attachment are appropriate for the stated light-duty use. issues.fix: Stain and clear-coat both faces and all edges of P1 while it is separate, allowing the finish to dry sufficiently before placing it on padding in step 7. Keep finish out of the connector pivots and slots, and allow the full specified cure time before using the table.

plan.title: Outdoor Slatted Garden Bench
plan.summary: A sturdy two-person outdoor bench inspired by the photo, with thick front-to-back seat slats, three horizontal backrest boards, a mortise-and-tenon seat frame, side aprons, and diagonal anti-racking braces. Finished dimensions are 1200 mm wide, 580 mm deep, and 850 mm high.
assumptions: The photo is interpreted as an outdoor slatted bench; the added backrest, side aprons, and braces make a safer, more rigid two-person build.
Dimensions are estimated from common bench proportions. Seat height is 450 mm; finished outer dimensions are exactly 1200 x 580 x 850 mm.

Use standard US home-center or local-lumberyard cedar stock, with common actual dimensions: 4x4 is 89 x 89 mm, 2x4 is 38 x 89 mm, 2x6 is 38 x 140 mm, and 1x4 is 19 x 89 mm. No special stock milling is required.
Choose straight, dry, exterior-rated cedar. The cut tenons, mortises, and slots are made from those standard finished sizes.
Use stainless or manufacturer-approved exterior-rated connectors and fasteners. The bench is freestanding on a level patio or deck and is not intended for climbing.

parts.name: Front legs
parts.notes: Cut from standard 4x4 cedar. The rear face is at z=70 mm; receive the front rail tenons in mortises on the inner x faces.

parts.name: Rear back-support posts
parts.notes: Cut from standard 4x4 cedar. The front face is at z=510 mm; receive the rear rail tenons on the inner x faces and attach backrest boards to the rear z faces.

parts.name: Front seat support rail
parts.notes: Cut from standard 2x4 cedar. Cut 25 mm-long, 12 mm-thick, 50 mm-high tenons at both ends; shoulders seat at x=89 and x=1111. Tenon portions overlap the legs intentionally.

parts.name: Rear seat support rail
parts.notes: Cut from standard 2x4 cedar. Cut 25 mm-long, 12 mm-thick, 50 mm-high tenons at both ends; shoulders seat at x=89 and x=1111. Tenon portions overlap the rear posts intentionally.

parts.name: Seat slats
parts.notes: Cut from standard 2x6 cedar. Slats run front-to-back, with 18 mm gaps and 46 mm side margins between the inner faces of the posts. Top of seat is y=450 mm.

parts.name: Backrest boards
parts.notes: Cut from standard 1x4 cedar. Boards span across the rear faces of both posts; top edge of the highest board is y=849 mm.

parts.name: Side aprons
parts.notes: Cut from standard 2x4 cedar. Each apron spans between the front leg and rear post on one side; ends meet the post/leg faces at z=70 and z=510.

parts.name: Diagonal side braces
parts.material: Cedar, actual 38 x 89 mm (nominal 2x4), ripped to 38 x 38 mm brace stock
parts.notes: Cut from standard 2x4 cedar by ripping to 38 x 38 mm and trimming each end to fit. Centerline length is 157 mm. Brackets connect the lower ends to the front legs and upper ends to the side aprons.

joints.drive_from: From the outside x face of each P1 leg, through the predrilled drawbore holes and into the P3 tenon.
joints.note: Glue the rail's 25 mm-long tenon into a matching 12 x 50 mm mortise in each leg. Clamp the shoulder tight and install two 10 mm hardwood pins per end; do not rely on glue on end grain alone.

joints.drive_from: From the outside x face of each P2 post, through the predrilled drawbore holes and into the P4 tenon.
joints.note: Glue the rail's 25 mm-long tenon into a matching 12 x 50 mm mortise in each post. Clamp the shoulder tight and install two 10 mm hardwood pins per end.

joints.drive_from: From the accessible x-facing sides of the front leg/apron joint, install one A35Z angle on each side of the apron and drive the approved screws into the leg and apron side grain.
joints.note: The apron end meets the leg face at z=70. Use two angles per joint, one on either side of the 38 mm apron, with the manufacturer-required screw pattern; no screws are driven into apron end grain.

joints.drive_from: From the accessible x-facing sides of the rear post/apron joint, install one A35Z angle on each side of the apron and drive the approved screws into the post and apron side grain.
joints.note: The apron end meets the rear post face at z=510. Use two angles per joint with the manufacturer-required screw pattern; no screws are driven into apron end grain.

joints.drive_from: From the x-facing side at the lower end of each brace, fastening the angle to the leg and brace side grain.
joints.note: Attach the lower end of each diagonal brace to its front leg with an exterior-rated connector and the manufacturer's specified screw pattern.

joints.drive_from: From the x-facing side at the upper end of each brace, fastening the angle to the apron and brace side grain.
joints.note: Attach the upper end of each diagonal brace to its side apron with an exterior-rated connector and the manufacturer's specified screw pattern.

joints.drive_from: From above through each seat slat into the front rail; use the round locating hole and the horizontal movement slot.
joints.note: No glue. At each rail/slat crossing, drill one 5 mm round locating hole at the slat's x center and one 8 x 18 mm slot 45 mm toward the same side, with the slot long axis across the slat width (x). Use washer-head screws; seat them snugly without crushing the wood or locking the slotted connection immovably.

joints.drive_from: From above through each seat slat into the rear rail; use the round locating hole and the horizontal movement slot.
joints.note: No glue. Use one 5 mm round locating hole at the slat's x center and one 8 x 18 mm slot 45 mm toward the same side, long axis across the slat width (x). Washer heads bear on the slat; tighten snugly without crushing the wood or immobilizing the slot.

joints.drive_from: From the rear z face of each backrest board into the side grain of each post, with screws normal to the board face.
joints.note: No glue or generic angle brackets. At each board/post crossing, use one 5 mm round locating hole near the board's vertical center and one 8 x 18 mm vertical slot 25 mm above it. Use structural washer-head screws rated for exterior use; the slot permits the backrest board's across-grain seasonal movement while both screws are securely seated.

consumables.name: Exterior-rated waterproof wood glue
consumables.note: Use only on the mortise-and-tenon rail joints.

consumables.name: Exterior wood filler
consumables.note: Optional for small surface defects; do not fill drainage gaps.

consumables.name: Sandpaper
consumables.note: Ease edges and prepare the cedar before finishing.

consumables.name: Exterior penetrating oil or outdoor stain
consumables.note: Apply to all faces and end grain; allow the label's full cure time before use.

tools.alternative: A hand brace and screwdriver; drill the round holes and cut slots with a narrow chisel.

tools.name: Router with straight bit and mortising guide
tools.alternative: A chisel and mallet with careful layout; make test cuts in scrap first.

tools.name: Chisels and mallet
tools.alternative: A router and guide for mortises, followed by a small chisel for cleanup.

tools.name: Clamps
tools.alternative: A helper can hold parts aligned while fastening; never hold a workpiece near a bit.

tools.name: Random-orbit sander
tools.alternative: Sanding block and hand sanding.

tools.name: Exterior-rated brush or finish applicator
tools.alternative: A clean cloth if the finish label permits cloth application.

steps.title: Buy and inspect standard stock
steps.text: Buy straight cedar boards in the listed standard actual sizes: 4x4 for P1/P2, 2x4 for P3/P4/P7/P8, 2x6 for P5, and 1x4 for P6. These are commonly stocked by US home centers and local lumberyards; no supplier milling is needed. Check boards for splits, twist, and decay, especially at the future mortises.
tools_used: Tape measure, pencil, and combination square
steps.tip: Ask the lumberyard to confirm actual board sizes before cutting; reject warped pieces for the long backrest boards.

steps.title: Cut and label the parts
steps.text: Crosscut all boards to the lengths and quantities listed, including the 545 mm seat slats and 1200 mm backrest boards. Rip the two brace blanks from 2x4 stock to 38 x 38 mm, then trim them to the listed 157 mm centerline length and fit their ends to the frame. Label every piece P1 through P8.
tools_used: Tape measure, pencil, and combination square
steps.safety: Wear eye and hearing protection. Support stock on both sides of each cut, clamp the guide, and keep hands clear of the blade.
steps.tip: Cut and test one seat slat first; use it as a reference only after verifying its length.

steps.title: Cut the rail joinery and movement holes
steps.text: Cut a centered 12 x 50 mm mortise, 25 mm deep, into the inner x face of each leg and rear post at the rail height. Form matching 25 mm-long tenons on both ends of P3 and P4, leaving shoulders that fit between the posts. Drill the pin holes through the legs/posts and tenons; also prepare the seat and backrest round holes and slots described in J7–J9.
tools_used: Router with straight bit and mortising guide
Drill/driver, bits, countersink, and slot-cutting bit
steps.safety: Clamp every workpiece before routing, drilling, or chiseling. Wear eye protection and hearing protection for powered tools; disconnect power before changing bits.
steps.tip: Test the tenon fit on scrap or offcuts. Aim for a snug fit that seats fully without forcing the leg or post apart.

steps.title: Assemble the front and rear seat rails
steps.text: Dry-fit P3 between P1 and P4 between P2, with both rail tops at y=412 mm. Apply exterior glue to the tenons and mortise walls, clamp the shoulders tight, and drive two 10 x 120 mm hardwood drawbore pins through each rail end; this makes J1 and J2. Keep the seat-support faces level and let the glue cure as directed on its label.
tools_used: Drill/driver, bits, countersink, and slot-cutting bit
steps.safety: Wear eye protection while drilling and installing pins. Keep fingers clear of clamps and wipe away squeeze-out before it hardens.
steps.tip: Check rail height and squareness before installing the pins; the front and rear rail tops must be in the same plane.

steps.title: Connect the side aprons and square the frame
steps.text: Fit each P7 apron between its front leg and rear post, with ends meeting at z=70 and z=510 mm and tops level with the seat rails. Install two Simpson Strong-Tie A35Z angles at each apron end, one on each x-facing side, using the specified #9 x 32 mm approved connector screws in the manufacturer's required pattern; this makes J3 and J4. Square the complete frame and check that it sits flat before tightening all connector screws.
tools_used: Drill/driver, bits, countersink, and slot-cutting bit
Tape measure, pencil, and combination square
steps.safety: Wear eye protection while driving connector screws and support the frame so it cannot tip.
steps.tip: Measure diagonally between opposite frame corners; matching diagonal measurements are a quick check that the frame is square.

steps.title: Install the diagonal braces
steps.text: Fit one P8 brace on each side, from the front leg at y=238 mm, z=70 mm to the underside of the apron at y=323 mm, z=202 mm. Fasten each end with one Simpson Strong-Tie A35Z angle and the specified approved #9 x 32 mm connector screws; this makes J5 and J6. Recheck that the frame remains square and that both braces bear firmly on their members.
tools_used: Drill/driver, bits, countersink, and slot-cutting bit
steps.safety: Wear eye protection and clamp each brace before drilling or fastening. Keep the bench stable while working on its sides.
steps.tip: The braces should sit tight without lifting the apron or twisting the leg; adjust their cut ends rather than pulling the frame out of square with screws.

steps.title: Attach the seat slats with movement allowance
steps.text: Lay the six P5 slats from z=0 to z=545 mm, with 18 mm gaps and 46 mm margins between the inner post faces. At each rail crossing, use one 5 mm locating hole at the slat's x center and one 8 x 18 mm slot 45 mm to the same side, with the slot running across the slat width. Drive two stainless #10 x 75 mm washer-head screws at each crossing, snug but not crushing the wood; this makes J7 and J8, with no glue.
tools_used: Drill/driver, bits, countersink, and slot-cutting bit
Tape measure, pencil, and combination square
steps.safety: Wear eye protection while drilling and fastening. Support the bench and keep hands clear of the driver bit.
steps.tip: Use an 18 mm spacer block between slats. Do not substitute countersunk screws in the movement slots; their tapered heads can lock the slot.

steps.title: Fasten the backrest boards
steps.text: Place the three P6 boards across the rear faces of P2 at y=560, 660, and 760 mm. At each post crossing, drill a 5 mm locating hole near the board's vertical center and an 8 x 18 mm vertical slot 25 mm above it. Drive two stainless #10 x 65 mm washer-head structural screws through each board into the post side grain, snug without crushing the board; this makes J9, with no glue.
tools_used: Drill/driver, bits, countersink, and slot-cutting bit
Tape measure, pencil, and combination square
steps.safety: Wear eye protection and support each long board while fastening. Check screw length on scrap to confirm no tip can break through a visible face.
steps.tip: The boards should sit flat against both posts. Keep each vertical slot centered under its washer head so it can accommodate seasonal width change.

steps.title: Sand and inspect the bench
steps.text: Ease sharp edges and splinters, starting with 80-grit and finishing with 120- and 180-grit paper. Inspect every mortise-and-tenon joint, bracket, screw head, drainage gap, and exposed end grain. Confirm that the bench stands level and does not rack when pushed gently from side to side.
steps.safety: Wear a dust mask and eye protection; collect sanding dust outdoors or with dust extraction.
steps.tip: Keep the gaps between seat slats clear so rainwater can drain.

steps.title: Apply the outdoor finish
steps.text: Brush or wipe exterior oil or stain over all faces, including the undersides of the seat slats and exposed end grain. Keep finish out of the drainage gaps and follow the product label for coats and cure time. Do not use the bench until the finish has cured as directed.
steps.safety: Work outdoors or with strong ventilation, wear gloves, and store or dispose of oily rags safely because they can self-heat.
steps.tip: Test the finish on an offcut first; cedar color and absorption vary.

safety_overview: Wear safety glasses for cutting, drilling, routing, and sanding; use hearing protection for powered saws and routers and a dust mask while sanding.
Clamp stock securely and support long boards to prevent movement, blade binding, or falling lumber.
Use only the specified exterior-rated connector system and compatible approved fasteners; verify screw lengths on scrap before installation.
Keep the slotted seat and backrest fasteners snug without crushing wood or locking the movement slots with countersunk heads.
Apply exterior finishes with ventilation and follow the product label. Store and dispose of oily rags safely.
This is a load-bearing bench for sitting, not climbing. Keep it on a level surface; if children may climb on it, secure it with rated anti-tip hardware into suitable structural material.

review.summary: The assembly sequence generally provides adequate tool access, but the bench needs a stronger, braced seat frame before it is suitable for two adults. Backrest connections, outdoor wood-movement details, and lumber sourcing also need revision.

issues.problem: J1 and J2 leave the seat rails supported only by pocket screws and glued rail ends. There are no side aprons or stretchers connecting the front legs to the rear posts; the seat slats become the only front-to-back ties. This is not an adequately braced frame for two adults, particularly when someone leans against the backrest or shifts sideways. Glue on the rail end grain is not a dependable substitute for structural joinery outdoors.
issues.fix: Revise J1 and J2 to use load-bearing housed or mortise-and-tenon rail connections, or a documented exterior seating-frame connector system. Add side aprons between each P1 front leg and P2 rear post, with structural connections at both ends, and diagonal corner bracing against racking. Install and square the complete frame before step 5. Add the new parts, joints, hardware, and joinery instructions to the plan rather than relying on extra pocket screws.

issues.problem: The backrest transfers a person's leaning load through unspecified 40 x 40 mm angle brackets and short screws embedded in thin cedar slats. Exterior rating establishes weather resistance, not structural capacity. Leaving ordinary slotted-bracket screws loose enough to slide also does not establish a secure backrest connection.
issues.fix: Specify a backrest connection intended to withstand leaning loads, including an identifiable connector, approved fasteners, and installation details. One practical revision is to mount the backrest boards across the faces of the posts, with suitable exterior structural fasteners into post side grain, rather than suspending their ends on generic angles. Revise P6 and J5 accordingly, and use properly detailed movement slots and washer-head fasteners where needed; do not instruct the builder simply to leave structural screws loose.

issues.problem: J3 and J4 glue each broad seat slat across its grain to the rails and additionally restrain it with two screws at each bearing. Outdoor wetting and drying will change the slat widths while the rail grain runs in the other direction. The continuous glue lines prevent that movement and can cause splitting or failed glue bonds.
issues.fix: Remove glue from J3 and J4 and revise the consumables notes accordingly. Specify movement-capable mechanical attachment: for example, one locating hole and one slot running across the slat width at each rail, with corrosion-resistant washer-head screws seated snugly without clamping the sliding connection immovably. Detail hole locations, slot dimensions, and fastener heads; do not use countersunk heads in the movement slots.

issues.problem: The plan requires exact finished cedar sections of 70 x 70, 25 x 145, and 19 x 75 mm without identifying suppliers or explaining how to produce them. These are not reliably available as standard finished stock at a typical US home center. The listed cutting instructions address lengths, not the ripping or thicknessing that some of these sections would require.
issues.fix: Provide actual purchasable stock specifications and suppliers, or revise the plan around locally available finished cedar sizes. If retaining these sections, specify supplier milling to the required cross-sections before step 1 and include its cost. Do not imply that ordinary crosscutting alone produces every listed part.

plan.title: Curved-Crest Wooden Chair
plan.summary: A sturdy, painted wooden chair inspired by the photo: four straight legs, a framed plywood seat, and a broad back panel with a raised, curved crest. The sculpted back is simplified to a jigsaw-cut panel rather than a carved or steam-bent part.
assumptions: The photo does not provide a reliable scale, so this plan uses an estimated adult chair size: 430 mm seat height and 800 mm overall height.
The backrest's curved, sculptural shape is approximated with a jigsaw-cut plywood outline; it will not have the thick, rounded, carved appearance of the photographed chair.

Use poplar for the legs and aprons, 25 mm birch plywood for the seat, and 18 mm birch plywood for the backrest. The finished chair is intended for one seated adult, but this home-built design is not load-tested or certified.
The bright orange appearance is approximated with orange enamel paint over primer.
The design uses straight, unsplayed legs and glued pocket-screw apron joints instead of turned legs and traditional Windsor-chair joinery.
clarifying_questions: Would you prefer this to be adult-size as planned, or scaled for a child?

parts.name: Front legs
parts.notes: Square-cut legs; sand edges lightly but keep the joint faces flat.

parts.name: Rear legs and back supports
parts.notes: These continuous rear legs support the backrest. Keep the full 800 mm height.

parts.name: Front apron
parts.notes: Fits between the front legs.

parts.name: Rear apron
parts.notes: Fits between the rear legs below the seat.

parts.name: Side aprons
parts.notes: The side aprons fit between the front and rear legs.

parts.name: Seat
parts.notes: Ease the edges after cutting. Rounded corners are a visual approximation; keep the seat's underside flat.

parts.name: Curved-crested backrest panel
parts.notes: The shaped panel sits on the rear faces of the rear legs. Cut the crest slowly and sand the curves smooth; this flat panel is not a carved or bent rail.

joints.drive_from: No screws. Clamp the front apron to the front face of each front leg while the glued tenon is seated.
joints.note: Cut a centered 8 mm thick x 25 mm high x 15 mm deep mortise in the leg face; locate it at y=372–397 mm. Form a matching 8 x 25 x 15 mm integral tenon on each apron end, leaving 5.5 mm shoulders on each side of the 19 mm apron thickness. Glue clean, unfinished mating surfaces.

joints.drive_from: No screws. Clamp the rear apron to the front-facing surface of each rear leg while the glued tenon is seated.
joints.note: Use a centered 8 x 25 x 15 mm mortise and matching integral tenon, with the mortise at y=372–397 mm. Glue clean, unfinished mating surfaces. Keep the mortise centered on the 45 mm wide face.

joints.drive_from: No screws. Clamp the front end of each side apron against the inside face of its front leg while the glued tenon is seated.
joints.note: Use a centered 8 x 25 x 15 mm mortise and matching integral tenon at y=372–397 mm. Center this mortise on the leg's inside x-face; this keeps it separate from the front-apron mortise on the adjacent z-face. Glue clean, unfinished mating surfaces.

joints.drive_from: No screws. Clamp the rear end of each side apron against the inside face of its rear leg while the glued tenon is seated.
joints.note: Use a centered 8 x 25 x 15 mm mortise and matching integral tenon at y=372–397 mm. Center this mortise on the leg's inside x-face, separate from the rear-apron mortise on the adjacent z-face. Glue clean, unfinished mating surfaces.

joints.drive_from: First drive three screws from the inside face of the front seat cleat horizontally into the side-grain face of P3. Then drive three screws upward through the cleat's vertical clearance holes into pilot holes in the underside of P6.
joints.note: Use one 16 x 19 x 420 mm poplar cleat, positioned inside P3 with its top flush with the apron top. The first three screws attach the cleat; the second three secure the seat. Do not glue the seat to the cleat; the plywood is stable, but the screw-mounted detail permits later removal.

joints.drive_from: First drive three screws from the inside face of the rear seat cleat horizontally into the side-grain face of P4. Then drive three screws upward through the cleat's vertical clearance holes into pilot holes in the underside of P6.
joints.note: Use one 16 x 19 x 420 mm poplar cleat, positioned inside P4 with its top flush with the apron top. The screws must not break through the visible outer face of the 19 mm apron or the top face of the seat. Do not glue the seat to the cleat.

joints.drive_from: For each side, first drive three screws horizontally from the inside face of the cleat into the side-grain face of P5. Then drive three screws upward through the cleat's vertical clearance holes into pilot holes in the underside of P6.
joints.note: Use one 16 x 19 x 380 mm poplar cleat on the inside face of each P5, tops flush with the apron tops. Keep the screw tips at least 3 mm inside the visible seat face and apron outer face. Do not glue the seat to the cleats.

joints.drive_from: From the rear face of P7 through predrilled holes into the side-grain face of each P2 rear leg.
joints.note: Apply a thin film of glue where the panel bears on the rear legs. Use four screws per leg, spaced vertically, with pilot holes; confirm the screw tips remain at least 3 mm inside the front face of the leg.

joints.drive_from: No fastener is driven at the apron corner; the adjoining apron edges meet at the corner while each apron is independently tenoned into the same leg.
joints.note: This is the corner seam/contact only, not a load-bearing apron-to-apron connection. Do not add a screw into apron end grain.

joints.drive_from: No fastener is driven at the apron corner; the adjoining apron edges meet at the corner while each apron is independently tenoned into the same leg.
joints.note: This is the corner seam/contact only, not a load-bearing apron-to-apron connection. Do not add a screw into apron end grain.

joints.drive_from: No direct fastener. P6 bears at the front-leg corner; the seat is secured to the frame through the apron-mounted cleats in J5 and J7.
joints.note: The corner contact is not a separate structural attachment. Do not drive a screw into the end grain of a leg.

joints.drive_from: No direct fastener. P6 bears at the rear-leg corner; the seat is secured to the frame through the apron-mounted cleats in J6 and J7.
joints.note: The corner contact is not a separate structural attachment. Do not drive a screw into the end grain of a leg.

steps.title: Source, verify, and mark the stock
steps.text: Ask a timber supplier to provide poplar legs surfaced to exactly 45 x 45 mm and apron boards surfaced to 19 mm thick, at least 140 mm wide. Rip the apron boards to 90 mm wide; do not substitute nominal stock without confirming its actual dimensions. Buy seat plywood supplied at an actual 25 mm thickness and backrest plywood at 18 mm; if the exact seat thickness is unavailable, stop and revise the seat and screw details before buying. Mark every part ID and keep the leg faces oriented consistently.
tools_used: Tape measure, combination square, and pencil
steps.safety: Have the supplier machine the solid wood if you do not have the equipment to surface it accurately. Use safe lifting practices when handling plywood sheets.
steps.tip: Check actual thickness with calipers or a reliable rule before laying out tenons, mortises, or screw lengths.

steps.title: Cut the legs, aprons, cleats, and panels
steps.text: Cut P1–P5 to their listed lengths and cross-sections. Rip and crosscut four poplar seat cleats: two at 16 x 19 x 420 mm and two at 16 x 19 x 380 mm; these are additional unmodeled support pieces, not replacements for any listed part. Cut P6 and P7 to their blank sizes, then trace and cut the rounded seat corners and curved backrest outline.
tools_used: Miter saw or circular saw with a straightedge guide
Jigsaw with a fine-tooth plywood blade
Tape measure, combination square, and pencil
steps.safety: Wear eye and hearing protection. Support sheet goods securely, keep hands clear of blades, and disconnect power before adjusting a saw.
steps.tip: The plywood must match its specified actual thickness; do not use a thinner panel and assume the existing screw details will still work.

steps.title: Machine the apron tenons and leg mortises
steps.text: At each apron end, cut an integral tenon 8 mm thick, 25 mm high, and 15 mm long, centered through the apron thickness and at y=372–397 mm in the assembled chair. Cut matching 8 x 25 x 15 mm mortises in the appropriate leg faces. Center each mortise on its 45 mm face; the front/rear mortises enter through the z-facing surfaces and the side-apron mortises through the x-facing surfaces, so the neighboring mortises do not intersect. Dry-fit every joint without glue and keep all mating surfaces clean and unfinished.
tools_used: Router with straightedge guide and 8 mm straight bit
Tape measure, combination square, and pencil
steps.safety: Wear eye protection and hearing protection for routing. Clamp parts securely, keep hands away from the cutter, and disconnect the router before changing bits.
steps.tip: Make a test mortise and tenon in matching scrap first; adjust for a snug fit that seats with hand pressure and light clamping, not hammering.

steps.title: Prepare the seat cleats and seat pilot holes
steps.text: On each of the four 16 x 19 mm cleats, drill three clearance holes for #8 screws, spaced evenly along its length and centered through the 19 mm height. Position the cleats against the insides of the aprons with their top edges flush with the apron tops; mark the matching screw locations on the aprons and drill pilot holes. Also mark three upward seat-screw locations per cleat and drill pilot holes in the underside of P6, stopping well short of its top face. Do not attach the cleats or seat yet.
tools_used: Tape measure, combination square, and pencil
steps.safety: Clamp each piece before drilling and wear eye protection. Use a depth stop or tape on the bit to prevent drilling through the seat.
steps.tip: The cleats sit inside the apron frame: the 420 mm cleats go on P3 and P4, and the 380 mm cleats go on the two P5 aprons.

steps.title: Glue and clamp the mortise-and-tenon frame
steps.text: Dry-assemble the four legs and four aprons, then confirm the frame is square and the feet sit in one plane. Apply wood glue to the clean mortise walls and tenons, seat P3 between P1, P4 between P2, and each P5 between a front and rear leg. Clamp each joint until its shoulders close; do not use pocket screws or screws into apron end grain. Check both frame diagonals before the glue sets.
tools_used: Tape measure, combination square, and pencil
steps.safety: Wear eye protection and keep fingers clear of closing joints and clamps. Get help to hold the frame steady if needed.
steps.tip: The front/rear and side mortises enter different faces of each leg; verify each apron is in its intended position before applying glue.

steps.title: Install the cleats and attach the seat
steps.text: With the frame upside down and the seat still off, attach each cleat to the inside face of its apron using three #8 x 32 mm screws through the cleat clearance holes into the apron pilot holes. The screws pass through 16 mm of cleat and penetrate 16 mm into the 19 mm apron, leaving at least 3 mm of wood before the outer face. Set P6 centered on the frame. Drive three #8 x 32 mm screws upward through each cleat into the seat pilot holes; they pass through 16 mm of cleat and penetrate 16 mm into the 25 mm seat, leaving 9 mm before its top face. Do not glue the seat to the cleats.
tools_used: Tape measure, combination square, and pencil
steps.safety: Support the frame securely before driving screws upward and wear eye protection. Use a depth stop and do not overtighten or strip the plywood.
steps.tip: The cleat tops must be flush with the apron tops so the seat rests evenly; verify this before fastening the seat.

steps.title: Fit and fasten the backrest
steps.text: Place P7 against the rear faces of P2, with its bottom edge at seat height and its crest aligned to the 800 mm overall height. Apply a thin film of glue at both leg contact areas and clamp the panel centered. Drive four #8 x 50 mm screws through the predrilled holes in P7 into each rear leg, checking that the tips remain at least 3 mm inside the front face of each leg.
tools_used: Tape measure, combination square, and pencil
steps.safety: Clamp the panel before drilling and wear eye protection. Keep the chair stable so it cannot tip while you work.
steps.tip: Predrilling reduces the chance of splitting the leg or bulging the plywood face.

steps.title: Fill and finish-sand
steps.text: Fill minor surface defects and the visible backrest screw recesses with paint-grade filler; do not fill the apron mortise shoulders or any structural glue line. Let the filler dry as directed, then sand with 120-grit and finish with 180-grit. Remove dust and check that all joints are tight and the chair does not rock.
steps.safety: Wear a dust mask and eye protection while sanding, and clean up dust before applying finish.
steps.tip: Correct any rocking before painting rather than trying to hide it with finish.

steps.title: Prime and paint
steps.text: Apply primer to all surfaces, including plywood edges, and let it dry as directed. Apply two thin coats of orange enamel, allowing the label's stated recoat time between coats. Keep the chair in a ventilated area while the finish dries.
steps.safety: Use ventilation and the protective equipment specified on the primer and paint labels. Keep finishes away from flames and ignition sources.
steps.tip: Thin coats are less likely to run on the curved crest and inside corners.

steps.title: Cure and inspect before use
steps.text: Wait for the paint to reach its full cure time; dry-to-touch is not the same as fully cured. Inspect the mortise-and-tenon joints, backrest screws, cleats, seat screws, and all four feet, then test gently on a level floor. Do not stand on the chair or use it as a step stool.
tools_used: Tape measure, combination square, and pencil
steps.safety: Keep the chair out of service until the finish is fully cured and the joints have been inspected.
steps.tip: Stop using the chair if a joint loosens, a screw backs out, or a part cracks.

safety_overview: Wear eye protection when cutting, drilling, and driving screws; use hearing protection around powered saws.
Wear a dust mask when sanding plywood or cured filler, and clean dust before painting.
Clamp work securely and keep hands away from blades and drill bits; unplug tools or remove batteries before adjustments.
Use primer and paint with good ventilation and follow their label instructions, including fire precautions and cure times.
This is a home-built chair intended for one seated adult, not a certified or load-tested product. Never stand on it or use it as a step stool.

review.summary: The assembly sequence is broadly workable, but the chair needs stronger apron-to-leg joinery, consistent cleat drilling instructions, and a corrected tool list before release.

issues.problem: The apron tenons are only 25 mm high with 15 mm embedment. These small joints are the chair's primary resistance to repeated side loads and backward leaning, with no stretchers or corner reinforcement. A snug initial fit does not provide adequate assurance against loosening under adult seating loads.
issues.fix: Revise J1–J4 to a proven chair-frame joint detail with substantially taller, deeper tenons and adequate surrounding leg material. Provide a revised drawing showing how neighboring tenons are accommodated without weakening the legs. Alternatively, specify a complete, proven reinforced chair-frame construction rather than relying on these short tenons alone.

issues.problem: The cleat instructions disagree about orientation: step 4 identifies a 19 mm vertical height, while step 6 describes the upward screws passing through 16 mm. Step 4 also explicitly drills only the horizontal clearance holes; it marks the upward locations but never directs the builder to drill vertical clearance holes through the cleats. Following this literally can leave the seat screws binding in the cleats instead of drawing the seat tight.
issues.fix: Add the four cleats to the parts list with IDs and an orientation drawing. Specify one installed orientation consistently in J5–J7 and steps 4 and 6, and select screw lengths and pilot depths for that orientation. In step 4, explicitly drill three horizontal attachment clearance holes and three vertical seat-screw clearance holes per cleat, offset so the two screw paths cannot intersect.

issues.problem: Step 3 requires a router, an 8 mm bit, chisels and a mallet, none of which appear in the main tool list. Conversely, the required pocket-hole jig is unused and its suggested bracket substitution does not match the specified joinery. A straightedge alone also does not explain how to support and guide the router safely on narrow leg faces.
issues.fix: Replace the pocket-hole-jig entry with the actual mortising and tenoning tools. Specify a clamped mortising jig with adequate router-base support, a suitable bit, chisels and mallet, and a defined tenon-cutting method such as a backsaw and shoulder-cleanup tools. Include jig setup and a scrap practice joint before machining chair parts.

issues.problem: Step 8 calls for filling backrest screw recesses, but J8 specifies washer-head screws and no counterbores. Washer heads normally remain proud; they should not be forced into plywood or buried under an unsupported mound of filler.
issues.fix: Either leave the washer heads exposed and paint them, removing the recess-filling instruction, or specify an appropriate recessed-head fastening detail with controlled recess depth and corresponding screw selection.

issues.problem: The frame starts upside down, then the instruction says to set the seat on the frame without explaining the change in orientation. The extended rear posts also make an unsupported upside-down chair awkward to hold while driving screws.
issues.fix: After attaching the cleats, place P6 face-down on a padded bench and position the inverted frame over it. Support the projecting rear posts clear of the bench edge, clamp the seat and frame together, and drive the seat screws from the accessible underside.

plan.title: Motorcycle Carburetor Service and Throttle Synchronization
plan.summary: General service workflow for an existing motorcycle fuel-metering assembly. This is not a fabrication plan: the single part entry represents the existing assembly being serviced, with an estimated envelope only. Carburetors and fuel-injected throttle bodies are different systems; confirm the exact motorcycle and follow its model/year service manual for disassembly, fuel-pressure relief, settings, and synchronization limits.
assumptions: This is a service procedure for an existing motorcycle, not a fabricated object. P1 is the existing fuel-metering assembly being serviced; its dimensions are a generic estimated envelope, not cutting dimensions or a claim about a specific motorcycle.

Assumes a multi-cylinder motorcycle with accessible carburetors or throttle bodies and a model-specific service manual available. Exact procedures, adjustment limits, and parts vary substantially by make, model, and year.
The terms “carburetor” and “throttle bodies” may refer to different fuel systems. Do not apply carburetor cleaning or adjustment instructions to an EFI system.
Cost is a rough estimate for typical consumables and a model-specific service or rebuild kit; it excludes tools, shop labor, and major damaged components.
Work outdoors or in a well-ventilated area, with the engine cold for fuel-system disassembly. Never run the engine indoors.
clarifying_questions: What are the motorcycle's make, model, and year?
Is it carbureted or fuel-injected, and how many cylinders, carburetors, or throttle bodies does it have?
What symptoms led to the repair, and do you already have a synchronization gauge and the model-specific service manual?

steps.title: Identify the fuel system and obtain specifications
steps.text: Record the make, model, year, engine code, and number of cylinders. Confirm from the service manual whether this is a carbureted system or EFI throttle bodies, then find the exact disassembly, fuel-pressure or float-level, and synchronization specifications. Do not proceed with adjustments if the system type or procedure is uncertain.
steps.safety: Do not guess at fuel-system settings; incorrect adjustments can cause fire, engine damage, or unsafe operation.
steps.tip: Take photos before removing hoses or linkages, but use the manual—not photos alone—to route them correctly.

steps.title: Prepare a safe work area
steps.text: Park the motorcycle upright on a stable surface outdoors or in a well-ventilated workspace. Let the engine cool completely, keep cigarettes, heaters, sparks, and open flames away, and have a suitable fire extinguisher within reach. Protect painted surfaces and keep an approved fuel container nearby.
tools_used: Eye protection, fuel-resistant gloves, and suitable fire extinguisher
steps.safety: Gasoline vapors ignite easily. Do not work near a pilot light, use a household vacuum near fuel, or run the engine in an enclosed space.

steps.title: Document and isolate the motorcycle
steps.text: Turn the ignition off and follow the manual's procedure for disconnecting the battery if required. Photograph and label fuel, vacuum, breather, and electrical connections before disturbing them. On EFI models, before any fuel-line connection is opened, follow the exact manual's fuel-pressure relief and fuel-pump isolation procedure in its specified order; keep fuel connections closed until that procedure is complete. Never loosen a fitting to release pressure. Obtain any model-specific equipment required by the manual before proceeding. Shut off the fuel supply where possible and drain fuel only into the approved container.
tools_used: Metric hand-tool set and screwdrivers that fit the fasteners
Small inspection light and labels or masking tape
steps.safety: EFI fuel may remain pressurized with the ignition off and can spray when a connection is opened. Avoid sparks, keep fuel away from hot parts, and clean up spills safely.
steps.tip: Label both ends of similar hoses; several hoses can look alike but have different functions.

steps.title: Inspect before disassembly
steps.text: Check for cracked intake boots, loose clamps, blocked air-filter parts, damaged hoses, fuel leaks, and loose electrical connectors. These faults can imitate poor synchronization, so correct them before tuning. If the manual calls for fuel-pressure or ignition checks, perform those checks before blaming the carburetors or throttle bodies.
tools_used: Small inspection light and labels or masking tape
steps.safety: Keep the engine off during visual inspection and do not test for fuel leaks with a flame.
steps.tip: A vacuum leak or ignition fault can make a synchronization adjustment misleading.

steps.title: Remove the carburetor assembly only if it is carbureted
steps.text: Follow the manual's order to remove the tank or airbox as needed, then disconnect and remove the carburetor assembly without forcing the intake boots or linkages. Keep the carburetors in cylinder order and protect open intake ports from debris. If the motorcycle is fuel-injected, skip carburetor disassembly and use the manual's EFI inspection procedure instead; do not open any EFI fuel connection until the pressure-relief and pump-isolation procedure in step 3 is complete.
tools_used: Metric hand-tool set and screwdrivers that fit the fasteners
Small inspection light and labels or masking tape
steps.safety: Fuel may remain in the assembly; keep it away from ignition sources and wear eye protection and fuel-resistant gloves. For EFI, never disconnect a pressurized fuel line.
steps.tip: Do not pull on throttle cables or twist a bank of carburetors against stiff intake boots.

steps.title: Clean and inspect carburetor components if applicable
steps.text: On a carbureted motorcycle, disassemble only as far as the manual directs and keep each carburetor's parts separated. Clean passages with compatible carburetor cleaner and gentle, regulated air only where permitted; do not enlarge jets or force steel wire through calibrated openings. Replace damaged seals or parts with the exact model-specific components, and use the manual's float-height method and specification.
tools_used: Metric hand-tool set and screwdrivers that fit the fasteners
Compressed air with a regulated nozzle
steps.safety: Cleaner can irritate skin and eyes and may be flammable. Use eye protection, gloves, and ventilation, and never direct compressed air at skin.
steps.tip: Lay parts out by carburetor and photograph each stage; swapping jets or small components between cylinders can create new problems.

steps.title: Reinstall and check for leaks and throttle return
steps.text: Reinstall the serviced carburetors, or reassemble EFI components, in the order and with the seals and torque values specified by the manual. Reconnect each labeled hose, cable, and connector, then with the engine off verify the specified throttle free play and smooth operation. Release the throttle from several open positions and confirm it returns promptly and fully to closed, including with the handlebars at both steering locks; correct any binding, cable-routing problem, or failed return before starting. Restore the fuel supply and check carefully for leaks before starting.
tools_used: Metric hand-tool set and screwdrivers that fit the fasteners
steps.safety: Keep the engine off while checking throttle operation and fuel leaks. If fuel appears or smells strongly, shut off the supply, ventilate the area, and do not start the motorcycle until the leak is fixed.
steps.tip: A pinched intake boot or misrouted vacuum hose can invalidate the synchronization.

steps.title: Connect the synchronization instrument
steps.text: With the engine off, connect the gauges or manometer to the exact vacuum ports identified in the service manual, using the specified restrictors or adapters. Route hoses away from the exhaust, fan, and moving parts. Leave any reference-cylinder or baseline adjustment as directed by the manual.
tools_used: Motorcycle carburetor/throttle-body vacuum synchronization gauges or manometer
steps.safety: Do not let gauge hoses contact hot exhaust parts or moving components. Secure loose clothing, hair, and tools before running the engine.
steps.tip: Check that all gauge hoses are connected and sealed before starting; an open vacuum port can cause erratic running.

steps.title: Synchronize using the correct system-specific procedure
steps.text: Start the engine and bring it to the manual's specified temperature and idle condition, using a cooling fan if the procedure requires extended stationary running. Adjust only the designated synchronization screws in small increments while comparing readings; do not turn throttle-stop, sealed, or factory-set screws unless the manual explicitly instructs you to. Follow the manual's target range and recheck idle after each adjustment.
tools_used: Motorcycle carburetor/throttle-body vacuum synchronization gauges or manometer
Metric hand-tool set and screwdrivers that fit the fasteners
steps.safety: Run the engine outdoors only. Keep hands, sleeves, gauge hoses, and tools clear of the hot exhaust, fan, and moving parts, and stop if fuel leaks or the engine overheats.
steps.tip: If readings will not stabilize or one cylinder is far outside the manual's range, stop and diagnose leaks, ignition, compression, or fuel delivery rather than forcing an adjustment.

steps.title: Verify operation and finish
steps.text: Shut the engine off before removing the gauges, then cap or reconnect every vacuum port as specified. Recheck fuel and intake leaks. With the engine off, verify the specified throttle free play and smooth operation; release the throttle from several open positions and confirm it returns promptly and fully to closed, including with the handlebars at both steering locks. Complete the manual's final idle and roadworthiness checks, and do not ride if there is a fuel leak, hanging idle, poor throttle return, or unresolved warning condition.
tools_used: Metric hand-tool set and screwdrivers that fit the fasteners
steps.safety: Let hot parts cool before handling them. Perform any test ride only after all covers and controls are secured and the motorcycle passes the manual's safety checks.
steps.tip: Record the final readings and any replaced parts so future diagnosis has a useful baseline.

safety_overview: Gasoline and cleaner vapors are highly flammable: work cold, ventilated, away from flames and sparks, and keep a suitable extinguisher nearby.
For EFI, relieve fuel pressure and isolate the pump exactly as the model-specific manual directs before opening any fuel connection; never loosen a fitting to release pressure.
Wear eye protection and fuel-resistant gloves; prevent cleaner, fuel, and compressed air from reaching skin or eyes.
Never run the motorcycle indoors. During synchronization, keep clear of hot exhaust, fans, and moving parts.
Use the exact model/year service manual. Do not adjust sealed throttle stops or guess at float levels, fuel pressure, or synchronization limits.
Stop and have a qualified motorcycle technician inspect the bike if there is a persistent fuel leak, damaged wiring, unstable engine operation, or a procedure beyond your experience.

review.summary: This is a service workflow rather than a fabrication plan. Its sequence is workable for an intermediate user following the exact motorcycle service manual. It appropriately separates carburetor and EFI procedures, requires pressure relief before opening EFI connections, and includes leak checks, throttle-return checks, outdoor engine operation, and clear stop conditions. No blocker or major issues identified; model-specific access, tools, and settings must be confirmed from the required manual before proceeding.

plan.title: Round Splayed-Leg Side Table
plan.summary: A 600 mm round plywood side table with four tapered legs splayed in both front and side views, matching the supplied drawing. The 25 mm top finishes at 550 mm overall height; an underside center cleat and angled leg-plate kits complete the assembly.
assumptions: The drawing's 600 mm diameter and 550 mm overall height are treated as exact targets. The top is 25 mm actual-thickness birch plywood, with its bottom at y=525 mm.

The four legs are interpreted as splayed diagonally in plan: each moves outward 65 mm in both x and z between its upper and lower center points. This gives about 7 degrees of splay in each front/side projection and about 10 degrees overall, matching the drawing.

The legs are bought as standard 533 mm (21 in) tapered round table legs, approximately 40 mm at the top and 28 mm at the foot, with M8 hanger bolts. Verify the leg and angled plate specifications before purchase.
The single 280 x 40 x 22 mm cleat is centered beneath the top, as suggested by the drawing. It is a center stiffener, not the primary support for the legs.

steps.title: Cut the round top and cleat
steps.text: Mark a 600 mm circle on P1 using a 300 mm radius trammel, then cut it carefully. Cut P3 to 280 x 40 x 22 mm and round its four corners to R20. Keep the saw base flat and avoid cutting past the line.

steps.title: Drill the cleat screw holes
steps.text: Stand P3 on its 22 mm-wide lower narrow face, with the 40 mm dimension vertical, and clamp it securely in a cradle. Mark four evenly spaced positions along its length, centered across the 22 mm face. Drill pilot holes along the 40 mm height through from the lower narrow face to the upper narrow face, and countersink only the lower face for the screw heads.

steps.tip: Label the four plate positions and their outward directions before turning the top over.

steps.title: Sand the parts

steps.safety: Wear a dust mask and eye protection, and connect dust collection or work in a well-ventilated area.
steps.tip: Avoid sanding a low spot into the plywood edge; keep the sander moving.

steps.title: Mask glue surfaces and apply finish

Follow the finish label for recoat and full cure times, then remove the masking immediately before assembly in step 6.
steps.safety: Ventilate the room, wear gloves and eye protection, and keep finish and finish-soaked rags away from flames; dispose of rags as directed on the label.

steps.title: Attach the center cleat

tools_used: Drill/driver with pilot bits and countersink

steps.title: Check and level the table

If one foot rocks, adjust it with a suitable furniture glide or have the foot corrected without changing the leg-plate angle. Allow the finish to reach its stated full cure before regular use.

steps.tip: Do not use the table as a seat or step; it is designed for ordinary side-table loads.

plan.title: Two-Step Wooden Step Stool
plan.summary: A compact, two-level stool inspired by the photo: contrasting hardwood treads sit between dark-painted plywood side supports. Intended for household stepping, not as a ladder or seat.
assumptions: Estimated from the photo; the finished stool is approximately 500 mm wide, 500 mm deep, and 450 mm high.
The stool is for one adult at a time on a flat, dry floor. This is a DIY build, not a certified or tested load rating; do not use it as a ladder.
Side supports are 18 mm birch plywood, painted dark. Treads are 25 mm edge-glued hardwood panels, such as oak or maple, with clear finish.
The upper tread has a 100 mm front overhang relative to the upper side-support ledge; it is secured at both side supports.
The image does not show exact dimensions or joinery, so the geometry and construction are practical approximations.
